extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, military administrators, and military legal officers (U.S. Army)
extracted.subtask_description: Authoritative administrative and legal standards governing desertion, deserter releases, and classifications/administration of military discharges (honorable, without honor, dishonorable), including procedural requirements, evidentiary rules, and revocation grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge classification (three kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of discharges into three kinds: the honorable, the discharge without honor, and the dishonorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification is recognized by the Executive branch (War Department) and is the framework for determining the character and consequences of separation from service. (References: multiple circulars and decisions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorable discharge — general presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless evidence to the contrary, a discharge is honorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For officers and enlisted men the default is honorable absent contrary evidence. An officer who resigns without stated reason or who fails an examination (absent evidence of culpable unfitness or fraud) is to be held honorably discharged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorable discharge — requirement of 'honest and faithful' service (enlisted men)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to an honorable discharge an enlisted man must have rendered the honest and faithful service stipulated in his enlistment contract and must occupy a status of honor at the instant of separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board of officers is called only in cases of discharge at expiration of enlistment; a consensus of company commander, board and convening authority is required to rate service as 'not honest and faithful.' Secretary of War has discretion to rate 'honest and faithful.' If service is 'honest and faithful,' honorable discharge must be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorable discharge — specific entitlement indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific facts that favor an honorable discharge: no derogatory remark on muster roll at muster out; soldier in hands of civil authorities may still receive honorable discharge; soldier sent away without discharge certificate entitled to honorable under circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deserter may receive honorable discharge if restored to duty or if imprisonment and return to duty lead to faithful service at term completion. Evidence on muster rolls and post-service behavior informs the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — nature and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Discharge without honor is a form of separation that is not technically dishonorable nor honorable; it is not a punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated in Army circulars but predates them; it recognizes separations that are not strictly honorable in fact. Important as an administrative classification, but War Department policy is conservative in its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — authorized circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances where discharge without honor may be given: (a) fraudulent enlistment, (b) discharged without trial on account of being disqualified for service physically or in character through his own fault, (c) discharge on account of imprisonment under civil court, (d) at time of discharge in confinement under sentence of general court-martial when dishonorable discharge is not provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the specified categories (from circulars and rules) under which a discharge without honor can be lawfully used. It should not be a device to avoid judicial process where trial is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — policy constraints and due process
rubrics_metrics.description: War Department policy is not to discharge without honor men charged with offenses that are triable by court-martial; discharge without honor is not to be used summarily to rid the service of undesirable soldiers without opportunity to defend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soldiers charged with sodomy or other serious offenses should be tried by competent courts; summary without-honor discharges without opportunity to present a defense are improper and may establish dangerous precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonorable discharge — method and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Dishonorable discharge may be given only by sentence of a general court-martial as a punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects noted: it terminates enlistments, involves loss of rights conditioned on honest and faithful service, and may terminate existing confinement as a soldier. (Text also notes it 'entails no disqualification for civil employment' per cited section—guidance should be read with context of cited authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of discharge — entitlement at expiration of enlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: Soldier is entitled to discharge at the expiration of his term of enlistment; a soldier cannot discharge himself; desertion does not operate as discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date rules include: actual separation date; notice (actual or constructive) constitutes discharge notice; special rules for soldiers sick in hospital or insane (with/without lucid intervals); rules for prisoners, those awaiting trial, commuted sentences, and commissioned officers (e.g., Senate nonconfirmation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of discharge — original as legal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The original certificate of discharge is legal evidence of discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters covered: who signs certificate; duplicates and parchment duplicates; second duplicates if original lost/destroyed; certificate of service furnished upon proof of loss or illegibility; situations where certificate lacking signature can later be completed. Certain statutory limits apply (e.g., section 224 R.S. limited to Civil War soldiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate character notation — 'character' entry and determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'character' notation on the certificate refers to character both as a man and as a soldier; boards and regulations are directory concerning the notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: board of officers called generally at expiration of term; consensus of company commander, board, and convening authority required to rate 'not honest and faithful'; Secretary of War has discretion; a nonfraudulent reenlistment of a dishonorably discharged soldier does not automatically render later service 'not honest and faithful.' If service is 'honest and faithful' an honorable discharge must be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executed discharge not revocable — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal executed discharge (honorable, dishonorable, or without honor) is not revocable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legal honorable discharge cannot be revoked and replaced by a dishonorable one, nor can a legal dishonorable discharge be revoked and an honorable one substituted. Orders purporting to revoke an executed discharge are unauthorized and illegal, though clerical errors or mistakes of fact may affect validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge may be revoked — grounds for revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds for revoking a discharge include: (A) secured by fraud, (B) insanity of soldier at time of discharge, (C) discharge given is of a different class than ordered (clerical or interpretive mistakes), (D) discharge issued by incompetent authority, (E) discharge may be revoked before execution by order, (F) if discharge issued while soldier is in civil custody and he is later finally acquitted, (G) illegal dishonorable discharge where sentence revoked, (H) revocation by act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fraud (discharge secured by agreeing to reenlist), insanity (if soldier insane and not in Government Hospital), incompetent authority (e.g., U.S. Commissioner issuing discharge), and timing (revocation possible before execution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deserter's release — not a discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: A deserter's 'release' relieves the soldier from liability to arrest and from trial and punishment by court-martial for desertion, but it is not a discharge certificate and is not evidence of discharge from the Army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Orders 55, 1890's description 'Release from the Army' is faulty; the release should be prepared to preclude any claim that its delivery operates as an actual discharge. Circular No. 5, A.G.O. (1894) explains purpose/effect: relieves government expense and protects deserters from arrest in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to secure a deserter's release
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper course for a deserter to secure a deserter's release: surrender to military authorities nearest his residence and apply to the Adjutant General with an affidavit stating he has remained constantly in the United States since desertion, supported by other affidavits as available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon establishment of these facts, a deserter's release issues as a matter of course (See C. 14163, July 11, 1911). The release relieves government from apprehension expense and protects deserter from arrest where the 103rd Article of War bars trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of war determination for desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for determining whether desertion occurred 'in time of war': desertion committed prior to exchange of ratification was held to be in time of war; when the U.S. is engaged in war with theater of operations outside U.S. territory, it is 'time of war' at home as well as abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions differentiate based on treaty ratification timing and theater-of-operations location to determine applicability of 'time of war' classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for government property lost due to desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier responsible for government property who deserts and the property disappears may remain financially responsible despite acquittal of stealing; loss found to be caused by desertion (board of survey) sustains government claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquittal of theft does not necessarily relieve officer/soldier from liability for disappearance of government property when desertion is found to have caused the loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's authority to drop officers from rolls after absence
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is authorized to drop from the rolls as a deserter any officer absent from duty three months without leave under section 1229 R.S.; when he does so and concludes the officer deserted, no court can review his decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: after being dropped pursuant to this authority the officer is fully separated from military service and becomes a civilian (statute of limitations considerations); dropping can have ineligibility implications for reappointment; legal complexities arise when later seeking trial under section 1230 R.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants who elope before enlistment — not deserters but criminal liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Under enlistment systems where applicants are not enlisted until reaching recruit depot, an applicant who, after being provided transportation and subsistence, elopes and does not report to the depot is not a deserter but may have violated the Criminal Code (embezzlement of U.S. property furnished for service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cases have resulted in prosecutions and convictions under section 5439 R.S.; sentences have varied (examples cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discharge without honor after conviction or trial — limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally improper to give discharge without honor to a soldier primarily on account of offenses for which he has been tried and acquitted, or for which he has been convicted and punished (unless procedural defects lead to mitigation/set-aside).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if soldier tried and acquitted, discharge without honor on same allegations is improper; if convicted and punished less than discharge, then later giving discharge without honor primarily for same offenses is improper. However, discharge without honor may be used when sentence is set aside due to procedural defects (C. 25915).
